scenario: AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to feel this way about my friends. Let me start by understanding the situation better. I just finished my freshman year in college, and I've managed to find a pretty good friend group. That's a big deal for me because I've always been really shy, so being part of a group means a lot. Now, here's the thing: in this group of eight, I'm the only one not in the school's Honors College. People, including my friends, have told me that this doesn't mean they're smarter or harder working than me, and I've tried to accept that. But the reality is, being in the Honors College gives them certain required courses that I don't have. So, they all have classes together without me. When we hang out, everyone talks about their classes, and I feel completely left out. It's like I'm not part of that shared experience. And now, I found out that next year, they're all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can't live there since I'm not in the Honors College, and I already feel left out enough. Now that they'll all live together, it's even more likely they'll end up hanging out without me just because they're all in the same place and might run into each other. How can I blame them for that? I tried talking to a couple of them about it, and one person said I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together. But I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they'd realize that seven people of an eight-person group living together is rather unfair. I don't want to have to start over and find new friends, but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. So, is it AITA (Ask aITA) to feel this way? Is it right or wrong for me to feel this way? Why? Alright, so to break this down, I need to consider a few things. First, is it reasonable for me to feel excluded when my friends are all in a situation that I'm not part of? Second, is it fair for me to expect them to make an effort to include me when their circumstances are different? Third, how much control do I have over this situation, and what can I do to improve it? Let's start with the first point: feeling excluded. It's natural to feel left out when your friends are all experiencing something you're not part of. Especially since we're talking about classes and living arrangements, which are significant parts of college life. It's understandable that I would feel excluded when the conversation revolves around experiences I'm not having. Now, moving on to the second point: expecting them to include me. It's a bit of a tricky balance. On one hand, I want to feel included and valued by my friends. On the other hand, they're in a situation that's different from mine, and it's not entirely their fault that we're not all in the same boat. It's also possible that they're excited about their new living arrangements and the opportunities that come with being in the Honors College, and they might not fully grasp how it makes me feel. The third point is about control and what I can do. I can't control where they live or what classes they take, but I can control how I approach the situation. Maybe I can find ways to stay connected with them despite the distance or the different classes. I could also consider reaching out to other friends or groups who are in a similar situation as me, which might help me feel more included. Another angle to consider is communication. I tried talking to one of them, but maybe I need to approach the conversation differently. Instead of making them feel bad, I could express how I'm feeling in a way that invites them to understand my perspective. For example, I could say something like, "I feel left out when we talk about your classes because I'm not having those experiences. Can we find ways to include me in our conversations?" It's also important to reflect on what I need from my friendships. Do I need friends who are in the same academic program as me, or can I value friendships that are based on other common interests or experiences? It might be helpful to explore other groups or activities where I can meet people who are in a similar situation, which could provide a sense of belonging and reduce feelings of exclusion. In summary, feeling excluded is a natural response to being in a different situation than your friends. Expecting them to make an effort to include you is reasonable, but it's also important to communicate your feelings in a way that encourages understanding rather than defensiveness. Additionally, exploring other avenues for friendship and connection can help mitigate feelings of exclusion and provide a more balanced social life. Now, considering whether it's right or wrong to feel this way. It's not a matter of right or wrong, but rather a matter of understanding and addressing the feelings in a constructive way. Feeling excluded is a valid emotion, and it's important to acknowledge it. However, it's also important to approach the situation with empathy and understanding, both for yourself and for your friends. In terms of whether it's AITA, it's more about how you handle the situation rather than whether it's inherently right or wrong to feel this way. If you approach the situation with open communication and a willingness to find solutions, it's more likely to be handled in a positive way. If you let these feelings fester without addressing them, it could lead to more significant issues down the line. So, in conclusion, it's not a matter of right or wrong to feel excluded in this situation, but it is important to address these feelings constructively by communicating with your friends, seeking understanding, and exploring other avenues for friendship and connection.
